hook: You know Paul says we are justified by faith apart from works. But did you know James says by works, and both of them point to Abraham?
story:
Two sentences, a few pages apart in the New Testament, look as if one was written to answer the other.

Paul, writing to the believers in Rome: “We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.”

James, in his letter: “You see then that by works a man is justified, and not only by faith.”

The same verb, justified. The same two words, faith and works. And then the strangest part: both writers prove their point with the same man and the same line of Scripture. Paul asks what Abraham found, and answers from Genesis: “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.” James quotes that very line, “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness,” but he sets it after another scene: “Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar?”

Read flat, one says apart from works and the other says not only by faith. So the question is fair. Is a person made right with God by faith alone, or not by faith alone? Readers have argued over these two verses for centuries. Yet Paul himself writes that James, Cephas and John, “those who were reputed to be pillars, gave to Barnabas and me the right hand of fellowship”.

voices.words: When Paul says that we are justified by faith, he means no other thing than that by faith we are counted righteous before God. But James has quite another thing in view, even to shew that he who professes that he has faith, must prove the reality of his faith by his works.

source.title: John Calvin, Commentary on James 2:20-26 (Christian Classics Ethereal Library)

moment:
Paul wrote Romans to a church he had not yet visited. “I long to see you,” he tells them. The question running through these chapters is whether the God of Israel accepts Gentiles without making them keep the law of Moses first. “Or is God the God of Jews only? Isn’t he the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also”. So when Paul turns to Abraham, he asks when Abraham was counted righteous: “Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.”

Paul also knew his message was being bent. In the same chapter he mentions people who claimed he taught “Let’s do evil, that good may come?” and he says such people are justly condemned. A few chapters later he asks the question himself, “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” and answers, “May it never be!”

The letter of James comes from another room. It is addressed “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion”, and in chapter 2 it rebukes a church that seats the rich man in a good place and tells the poor man to stand. Then comes the picture behind its words on faith: a brother or sister “naked and in lack of daily food”, and a believer who says, “Go in peace. Be warmed and filled;” and gives nothing. James asks, “what good is it?”
around:
Right after the verse, Paul guards it from being read the wrong way: “Do we then nullify the law through faith? May it never be! No, we establish the law.” In another letter he says that what counts is “faith working through love.”

James, for his part, never says faith does not matter. He puts it as a challenge: “Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works.” Faith and works belong together: “You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected.” The faith he attacks is one that a man “says he has” and that does nothing, the kind of believing of which he says, “The demons also believe”. His second example is not a law-keeper at all but Rahab, who was “justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way”.

The two writers also mean different works. For Paul in Romans 3 and 4 they are “the works of the law”, with circumcision as his example. For James they are a coat for the cold, food for the hungry, Abraham’s obedience and Rahab’s help.
after:
In Acts, Paul and James meet in Jerusalem. When some taught Gentile believers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved”, the church met in Jerusalem, and James gave the judgment: “we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God”. Years later Paul came back to Jerusalem and “went in with us to James; and all the elders were present.” He told what God had done among the Gentiles, and they “glorified God.” Tradition holds that the letter was written by James the brother of the Lord, whom Paul met in Jerusalem; modern scholars often think someone wrote it later in his name.

The two sentences went on working long after. Augustine of Hippo warned against readers who took Romans 3:28 as leave to live badly. In 1522 Martin Luther set James among four books he placed apart at the end of his New Testament, after the books he counted as chief. On January 13, 1547, the Council of Trent, in its decree on justification, quoted James 2:24 to teach that the justified grow in justice through good works.

Then, on October 31, 1999, in Augsburg, the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification. Together they confessed that people are accepted by God by grace alone, through faith in Christ’s saving work and not because of any merit of their own, and that the Holy Spirit renews their hearts and calls them to good works. Methodists signed it in 2006, and the Reformed churches and the Anglican Communion in 2017. The Virtual Museum of Protestantism describes it as a differentiated consensus: agreement was reached, while various interpretations remain.
readings:
Readers have set these verses side by side in several ways.

One reading looks at the word justified. Calvin argued that Paul means being counted righteous before God, while James means showing that faith is real. Bible Hub’s Greek lexicon puts it in one line: Paul speaks of the basis of justification before God, James of its demonstration before people.

A second reading looks at faith. The faith James rejects is a faith someone only says he has, the kind demons have too. The faith Paul praises in Abraham is a trust that “grew strong through faith, giving glory to God”. On this reading the two men are not using the word for the same thing.

A third reading looks at works. Paul shuts out the works of the law as the way in; James asks for the mercy that living faith does. On this reading James 2 answers people who had heard Paul and concluded that it did not matter how they lived, the danger Paul himself warns about in Romans 3 and 6. Augustine read it this way, and some in the modern debate think James is answering a misunderstanding of Paul.

Others think the two letters really differ. Martin Luther judged that James contradicts Paul, though he praised the letter for teaching God’s law. Some scholars think the passage is a response to Paul himself, not to his misreaders. And Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox teaching has historically read the passage as disproving simplistic versions of justification by faith alone. Each tradition still reads the two verses in its own way.
argued:
The argument is old. Augustine of Hippo wrote of readers of Romans 3:28 who [[augustine]] He answered them with Paul’s own words about faith that works by love, and with the line from James about demons who believe.

In 1522, when Martin Luther published his German New Testament, he wrote a preface to James. He praised the letter for teaching God’s law but said it was not written by an apostle, because on justification [[luther]] Abraham, he pointed out, was counted righteous in Genesis 15, before he offered Isaac. Even so, Luther granted that the writer meant to warn people who trusted in a faith without works.

John Calvin answered that the clash lies in one word used two ways: [[calvin]]

The Council of Trent quoted James 2:24 in its own decree on justification, and four and a half centuries later Lutherans and Catholics signed a common statement on the heart of the matter. The argument has calmed, but it has not ended.
point: Side by side, the two verses use the same words for different things. Paul is answering whether a person must keep the law of Moses to be made right with God, and he says no: trust God, as Abraham did. James is answering whether a faith that speaks kindly and leaves a hungry brother hungry is faith at all, and he says no: real faith shows in what it does, as Abraham’s did. Whether that makes them two halves of one truth or two views that truly differ is the question their readers still answer in different ways.
lesson:
These two letters ask you two different questions, and you may need both.

Paul asks what you are standing on. If you have been trying to earn God’s acceptance, keeping score of your good days and your bad ones, Romans says God counts righteousness to the one “who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly”. You can stop trying to pay your own way in.

James asks what your faith is doing. Is there someone near you who is cold or hungry or alone, someone you could help this week and not only wish well? James says a faith that answers need with kind words and nothing more is dead.

You do not have to choose one letter over the other. You could read Romans 4 and James 2 on the same day, slowly, and ask God which one you need to hear more right now. And if you do not share this faith, the two letters still say something many people recognize: what we trust in and what we actually do belong together.

echoes.note: Paul himself says that what counts is “faith working through love.” The faith Paul preaches and the works James asks for meet in one line.
A letter in Paul’s name asks that “those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works.” Believing comes first, and good works are expected to follow.
John asks how God’s love can remain in someone who sees a brother in need and closes his heart, and ends: “let’s not love in word only”. It is the picture James paints in chapter 2.
